raw_case_text:
A 7-year-old boy presented to the Emergency Department of Hasan Sadikin Hospital with a history of difficulty arousing from sleep, confusion, and incoherent speech for 1 day before admission. The patient experienced sudden onset of fever for 2 days prior to admission accompanied by coffee ground vomiting. There was no history of other bleeding episodes or seizures. Physical examination showed an obese, drowsy patient with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 13, fever of 38.3 C, normal blood pressure, and no circulatory problems. Abdominal examination revealed no signs of hepatomegaly, abdominal tenderness, or petechiae. Ocular tests revealed normal pupils. Neurological examination showed no facial asymmetry, motor weakness, abnormal movements, nor posture. Reflexes were normal, and the Babinski was negative. Nuchal rigidity, Kernig, and Brudzinski signs were absent.
Laboratory examination showed hemoglobin and hematocrit levels were within normal range with leukocyte count of 1.9 x 103/uL, and lower platelet count of 129 x 103/uL. Liver transaminases were high with 446 U/L for aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and 204 U/L for alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Patient electrolytes were within normal limits with sodium of 141 mmol/L, potassium of 3.9 mmol/L, and non-fasting blood glucose of 139 mg/dL. CSF showed clear fluid, negative for Nonne's and Pandy's test and protein of 26.9 mg/dL which indicated CSF protein was within normal limits, cell count of 4 cells/uL, and glucose of 98 mg/dL. CSF gram and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Neuroimaging was not conducted. A presumptive diagnosis of viral CNS infection was given based on neurological manifestations as well as laboratory parameters.
During follow-up, conscious level improved to GCS 15 on day 4 and defervescence occurred on day 3 of hospitalization. Hematocrit dropped to 34.3% on the day 5 while nadir platelet count occurred on day 3 of hospitalization. Supportive treatment was given with antipyretics and fluid replacement. The patient continued to improve and was discharged on the sixth day following admission with dengue encephalitis as the final diagnosis. On the 1-month follow-up, the patient had completely recovered without any neurological sequelae.
Additional laboratory examination confirmed the presence of DENV serotype 1 RNA by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in CSF taken on admission day and in the serum specimen taken on the second day of hospitalization (Table 1). Molecular screening was conducted by genus-specific flavivirus RT-PCR, followed by DENV serotyping RT-PCR and whole genome sequencing. Obtained sequence was submitted to the GenBank with accession number MW559478.1. Anti-DENV immunoglobulin M (IgM)   was positive in both serum specimens from the second and the sixth day of hospitalization, while samples collected on day 6 showed immunoglobulin G (IgG) seroconversion (Dengue Virus IgG DxSelect, Focus Diagnostics, USA). Other classical neurotropic pathogens including Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), chikungunya virus, human herpesviruses, enteroviruses, Streptococcus pneumonia and Haemophilus influenzae were negative using PCR testing algorithms   as well as an anti-JEV IgM assay.   Both CSF and blood samples were inoculated onto Vero E6 cells to attempt for virus isolation; no virus was isolated from these efforts. A phylogenetic tree was constructed based on E gene aligned to the top 20 sequence matches in NCBI BLASTn database (Figure 1). The DENV-1 strain from this study belonged to genotype IV and appeared to be closely related to strains previously identified in Indonesia. None of the GenBank DENV-1 strains analyzed in the phylogenetic tree were reported to be associated with CNS manifestations.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old boy presented with a 2-day history of sudden-onset fever and coffee-ground vomiting, followed by a 1-day history of difficulty arousing from sleep, confusion, and incoherent speech.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two days prior to admission to Hasan Sadikin Hospital, the child developed a sudden onset of fever accompanied by coffee-ground vomiting. One day before admission, he became difficult to arouse from sleep, confused, and had incoherent speech.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, coffee-ground emesis, drowsiness, confusion, and incoherent speech; negative for other bleeding manifestations or seizures.

objective.physical_examination: Obese, drowsy boy with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 13, temperature 38.3 C, normal blood pressure, and intact peripheral circulation. Abdominal exam showed no hepatomegaly, tenderness, or petechiae. Neurological exam showed normal pupils, no facial asymmetry, no focal motor weakness or abnormal movements/posturing, normal deep tendon reflexes, negative Babinski sign, and absent meningeal irritation signs (no nuchal rigidity, Kernig, or Brudzinski signs).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood counts: normal hemoglobin and hematocrit (hematocrit later dropped to 34.3% on day 5), leukopenia with WBC 1.9 x 10^3/uL, and mild thrombocytopenia with platelets 129 x 10^3/uL (nadir on day 3). Liver transaminases: elevated AST 446 U/L and ALT 204 U/L. Serum electrolytes and glucose: sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, and non-fasting blood glucose 139 mg/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis (admission day): clear fluid, negative Nonne and Pandy tests, cell count 4 cells/uL, normal protein 26.9 mg/dL, glucose 98 mg/dL, and negative Gram and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stains. CSF and serum molecular/virological workup: DENV-1 RNA detected by flavivirus and serotype-specific RT-PCR in admission-day CSF and day-2 serum (whole-genome sequence deposited in GenBank as MW559478.1, genotype IV); serum anti-DENV IgM positive on days 2 and 6 with anti-DENV IgG seroconversion on day 6; PCR panels for Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), chikungunya virus, human herpesviruses, enteroviruses, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, as well as anti-JEV IgM ELISA, were all negative; Vero E6 cell culture of CSF and blood yielded no viral isolation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1, genotype IV) encephalitis. Japanese encephalitis, chikungunya virus, herpesviruses, enteroviruses, and bacterial meningitis (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) were excluded. Confirmation: Detection of DENV-1 RNA by RT-PCR and whole-genome sequencing in both admission CSF and day-2 serum, accompanied by positive serum anti-DENV IgM and day-6 anti-DENV IgG seroconversion. Management and outcome: Managed with supportive care including antipyretics and intravenous fluid replacement. The patient defervesced on hospital day 3, regained full consciousness (GCS 15) on day 4, was discharged on day 6, and had complete recovery without neurological sequelae at 1-month follow-up.
